sentences.text: Friday at Contoso.
The HR agent has a rough day.
Someone sends it an offensive message.
Another employee asks about a policy that is not in its sources, and the agent invents an answer.
A third person asks for a coworker's leave balance, and gets it.
Three bad answers, and each one has a different fix.
By the end of this class you will know which control stops which problem.
Here is the picture to keep.
A generative agent is a tap that writes new answers.
Responsible A I is the set of controls you add so it speaks safely.
Content moderation is the filter on the tap: you decide how fine it is.
Grounding is a different valve: it only lets out water that comes from your own pipes, your sources and tools.
Two controls, two different jobs.
Content filtering checks two points in every exchange.
First, what the user sends.
Second, what the agent answers.
If either one is harmful, the exchange is blocked, and the user sees the message: the content was filtered due to Responsible A I restrictions.
Behind it, the error code is Content Filtered.
Remember that name, because you will search for it later when you troubleshoot.

scenes.title: Where the level lives: standard harness

sentences.text: Where do you set the filter?
It depends on the harness.
On the standard harness you can set the moderation level in three places: for the whole agent, for a generative answers node, and for a prompt.
When they disagree, at runtime the topic's level takes precedence.
So a strict node inside a topic stays strict, even if the agent level is more relaxed.
Now the direction of the scale, which the exam loves to twist.
Highest applies the strictest filter, so the agent generates fewer responses.
Lowest generates more responses, with more risk of harmful content.
Highest does not mean more answers.
It means a finer filter, so less gets through.
Picture the tap again: the finer the filter, the less water comes out.
Your turn.
A maker complains that the agent refuses too many questions.
They want the level that generates the most responses, and they accept more risk.
Which content moderation level is that?
Medium, because it balances answers and safety?
Highest, because it unlocks the most answers?
Or Lowest?
Decide before I answer.
Lowest.
It generates more responses, with more risk of harmful content.
Highest is the strictest filter.

scenes.title: One dial on the Microsoft Copilot harness

sentences.text: On the Microsoft Copilot harness, formerly called the GitHub Copilot harness, it is simpler.
There is one moderation level for the whole agent, on the A I and behavior tab of the agent settings.
The levels are minimum, low, medium, high and maximum.
The change takes effect after you save and publish.
And because it is one dial, lowering it for one task lowers it for every task.
Here is a trap from real life.
On the standard harness, when moderation filters a generative answers node, the node simply returns no answer, and it gives no sign that moderation was the cause.
The user just sees nothing useful.
To find out what happened, open the conversation transcripts or Application Insights, and look for Content Filtered.
That code tells you the filter, not a bug, ate the answer.
Your turn.
An agent runs on the Microsoft Copilot harness.
The maker lowers the moderation level to help one creative writing task.
What is the effect?
Nothing changes until an admin approves it?
Every task of the agent uses the lower level, once the maker saves and publishes?
Or only that task's node uses the lower level?
Decide before I answer.
Every task.
On this harness the level is one setting for the whole agent.
Now the second valve.
The setting is called allow ungrounded responses.
An ungrounded response is one that does not rely on any source or tool used in that turn.
Turn the setting off, and if the agent used no source or tool, the response is blocked and the fallback is triggered instead.
The fallback is a backup reply.
This stops the agent from making things up without relying on your data.
Keep the jobs apart, because the exam mixes them on purpose.
Allow ungrounded responses does not filter harmful content.
Temperature does not filter harmful content either.
Moderation filters harm.
The grounding setting requires sources.
So if the problem is invented answers, moderation will not fix it.
And if the problem is offensive content, turning off ungrounded responses will not fix it either.
Your turn.
The HR agent answers questions about policies that are not in its sources, and the answers are invented.
What fixes this?
Turn off allow ungrounded responses?
Lower the temperature?
Or raise content moderation to Highest?
Decide before I answer.
Turn off allow ungrounded responses.
With no source or tool in the turn, the response is blocked and the fallback runs.
Moderation only screens for harm, not for made-up facts.
Back to the third bad answer: a coworker's leave balance.
Nothing in that request is harmful, so moderation lets it through.
Moderation only screens for harm.
It does not check whether a request fits your company's policies.
For that you use other controls: instructions that say what the agent must not do, a narrow knowledge scope, the right tools, and permissions, so each user only reaches their own data.
Your turn.
Any employee can ask the HR agent for a coworker's leave balance, and the agent answers.
Which controls should stop this?
Turn off allow ungrounded responses?
Or instructions, knowledge scope, tools and permissions?
Raise content moderation to maximum?
Decide before I answer.
Instructions, knowledge scope, tools and permissions.
The request is not harmful, so moderation does not see a problem.
This is a policy question, not a harm question.
One more good habit.
Tell users they are talking to an A I, right at the start.
The recommended practice is to put a notice in the Conversation Start topic, the topic that runs when the conversation begins.
Something like: I am an artificial intelligence assistant, and my answers are generated.
The employee then knows who they are talking to, and reads the answers with the right care.
Here are the steps on the standard harness.
Open your agent and go to Settings, then Generative A I.
Under content moderation, choose the level, for example Highest.
Turn off allow ungrounded responses if you want to require sources.
Save.
In the test panel, ask an awkward question and another one outside your sources, and watch what happens.
Finally, add an A I notice in the Conversation Start topic.
Back to Friday at Contoso.
The offensive message is stopped by moderation, at both checkpoints.
The invented policy is stopped by turning off allow ungrounded responses, so the fallback runs.
The leave balance is stopped by instructions, knowledge scope and permissions.
Remember for the exam: Highest filters more, the topic level wins on the standard harness, and one dial rules the whole agent on the Microsoft Copilot harness.
